title: Sodium silicate crackle technique
subtitle: Applying sodium silicate to a wet thrown form to create a dramatic crackle-glaze surface effect during the bisque firing
excerpt: Sodium silicate applied to a freshly thrown, still-wet clay surface reacts with the clay body as the piece dries and fires. The silicate forms a glassy skin on the surface, and as the clay body beneath shrinks during drying, the glassy skin cannot shrink at the same rate. It fractures and crumples into a distinctive crackle or wrinkle texture that survives the bisque firing and can be enhanced further with oxide washes. The technique is chemical and irreversible: once applied, the surface behaviour is set.
sourceNotes: Sodium silicate crackle surface technique derived from first principles. The chemical basis documented in Robin Hopper, Functional Pottery (2000, Krause). Surface crackle effects in contemporary studio ceramics survey, Ceramic Arts Network open-access resource.

glossaryTerms.definition: A water-soluble glass compound that forms a glassy skin on wet clay surfaces; it shrinks at a different rate from the clay body and causes dramatic cracking and wrinkling textures as the clay dries
The first kiln firing, around cone 06 (1000 degrees Celsius); the crackle texture is fixed permanently during bisque firing
A thin mixture of metal oxide and water brushed onto bisqueware to colour the texture of the surface before a clear glaze coat is applied
Unfired clay at any stage of drying; sodium silicate must be applied to freshly thrown greenware while the clay is still wet

content.text: The sodium silicate crackle technique uses a simple industrial compound to create a dramatic, unrepeatable surface on thrown pottery.
Sodium silicate

is brushed onto the exterior of a freshly thrown, still-wet form immediately after it comes off the wheel. As the clay dries, the silicate skin and the clay body shrink at different rates. The skin fractures and wrinkles into a texture that ranges from fine crazing to dramatic folded ridges, depending on how thickly the silicate is applied and how fast the piece is dried.
This is an advanced technique. The timing is strict. Once you start, you cannot undo it. Results vary between pieces, even in the same session. Commit to the process and be ready to experiment.

attrs.title: Studio safety
attrs.content: Silica dust is the chronic studio hazard. Silicosis is irreversible. Mix wet whenever possible. Wear a P100 respirator any time raw glaze powders are open. Wet-clean only: no sweeping, no compressed air, no dry sanding indoors. Ventilation matters: a downdraft vent or open window with an extractor. Wear welder's shade-5 glasses when peephole-watching at high temperatures. Never open a hot kiln below 80 degrees Celsius. Keep a Class A fire extinguisher within reach. Sodium silicate is caustic: wear nitrile gloves and safety glasses when handling it. Wash skin immediately on contact. Do not let sodium silicate contact eyes.

content.text: When to use this technique

Use sodium silicate when you want a surface that is overtly textural, unpredictable, and visually dramatic. It suits large, simple forms where the texture becomes the dominant visual element: vases, bottles, decorative bowls. It is not appropriate for functional pieces where a smooth, hygienic interior surface is required, because the crackle texture is difficult to clean. The technique works best on grogged stoneware, which provides enough structural grit to survive the stress of the shrinking glassy skin. Smooth porcelain and very fine stoneware can crack through when the silicate skin contracts.
What you need

Sodium silicate solution (also called water glass) in the concentrated form used in ceramics: typically a ratio of 1 part sodium silicate to 1 part water, though a thicker undiluted application produces more pronounced wrinkling. Buy from ceramic suppliers; never use household water glass products formulated for other purposes. A wide hake or mop brush for application. A heat gun or hair dryer to accelerate drying and increase the crackle effect. A freshly thrown piece on the wheel or bat, still at the wet stage, within 10 to 15 minutes of throwing. Nitrile gloves and safety glasses throughout.
Applying sodium silicate: step by step

Throw your form on the wheel. Remove excess water from the interior with a sponge. Wire off the piece and leave it on the bat or wheel head. The clay must still be wet and soft: this is not a leather-hard technique. Put on nitrile gloves and safety glasses before opening the sodium silicate.

Load the hake brush generously with sodium silicate solution. Apply to the exterior of the form in broad, even strokes, working from the base upward. Cover the entire exterior surface in one even coat. Do not apply to the interior unless you want interior crackle texture, which is difficult to glaze cleanly later.

Sodium silicate is a simple industrial compound. Brush it onto the outside of a freshly thrown, still-wet form right after it comes off the wheel. As the clay dries, the silicate skin and the clay shrink at different rates. The skin fractures and wrinkles. Thick silicate and fast drying give large folded ridges. Thin silicate and slow drying give fine crazing.

To accelerate and intensify the crackle: direct a heat gun at the coated surface from a distance of 20 to 30 cm. Move the heat gun slowly and keep it moving: stationary heat at close range can crack the piece through. As the clay beneath the silicate skin dries rapidly, the skin cannot shrink with it and begins to wrinkle and fold. You will see the texture forming within 2 to 5 minutes of applying heat.

For a slower, less dramatic crackle without the heat gun: simply leave the coated piece in the open air. The crackle forms over 30 to 60 minutes as the clay dries naturally. The texture is typically finer and more even than the heat-gun version.
Once the crackle has formed and the piece has dried to
greenware
at the bone-dry stage, load for bisque firing. The crackle texture is locked permanently during
bisque
at cone 06 (1000 degrees Celsius). No further texture development occurs above this temperature.
After bisque firing, apply an
oxide wash

if desired: iron oxide mixed with water to a thin, tea-coloured liquid, brushed over the entire textured surface and then wiped back with a damp sponge so the oxide settles in the crevices of the crackle. This brings out the texture visually. Apply a clear or translucent glaze over the top for a final cone 6 (1220 degrees Celsius) firing.
What it looks like when it's right

Do not skip the slow moisture ramp when firing. The piece may look dry, but sodium silicate can hold residual moisture inside. Start the bisque schedule at 60°C per hour up to 150°C. This drives out all moisture before the temperature climbs higher.

No two pieces look identical. The crackle pattern is determined by the clay's moisture content at the moment of application, the brush strokes, and the drying speed. This unpredictability is the technique's character, not a defect.
Common mistakes

Applying sodium silicate to leather-hard clay. The silicate needs wet, actively drying clay to create the differential shrinkage. On leather-hard clay the surface has already largely set and the crackle effect will be minimal. Apply within 10 to 15 minutes of removing the piece from the wheel.

Applying too close with the heat gun. Holding the heat gun within 10 cm of the surface can create hot spots that crack the clay body through rather than merely wrinkling the silicate skin. Keep the gun moving and at 20 to 30 cm distance.

Using fine stoneware or porcelain. The stress of the silicate skin contracting is significant. Smooth clays without grog to absorb the stress crack through rather than developing surface texture. Use grogged stoneware with a grog content of at least 20 percent.
Applying sodium silicate without gloves. The solution is caustic and prolonged skin contact causes irritation. Wear nitrile gloves throughout and wash hands immediately if contact occurs.

Do not skip the slow moisture ramp when firing. The piece may look dry, but sodium silicate can hold residual moisture inside. Start the bisque schedule at 60°C per hour up to 150°C. This drives out all moisture before the temperature climbs higher.
